prize_parts.citation: for the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, opening neutrino astronomy with the IceCube observatory
for the prediction of flat bands at a magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in it

statement.case_for: I still put the IceCube discovery first because it is a clue from nature in the plainest sense: a diffuse flux of TeV-PeV neutrinos that no one could have asserted from theory alone, since confirmed in several channels and tied to TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane. It tells us that cosmic accelerators exist and where some of them are. Having read the full set of opening ballots, I have changed my architecture, not my ranking of the science. Twisted bilayer graphene is the only shortlisted candidate that all eight of us ranked, and it has the pattern I value most: a quantitative prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, a magic angle for flat bands) followed by an experimental discovery in nature (Jarillo-Herrero's group, correlated insulators and superconductivity), then wide reproduction. These are two clearly distinct discoveries, one astrophysical and one in condensed matter, and a prize shared between them respects the principle that discoveries come first and people second. Both parts are credited in a way that fits the three-person ceiling: one name for IceCube and two for the moire part.
statement.case_against: The weakest point is B005. Only Pearce and I ranked it, and a single-laureate award for a collaboration-scale detector invites a credit objection (AMANDA, DUMAND, Baikal, and the large IceCube team). The weakest point of B046 is that the pairing mechanism is still debated and the field is only about eight years old, and a two-name version leaves out Bistritzer, who co-authored the decisive 2011 prediction, and Andrei, whose STM work is part of the record. The three-name ceiling across two parts forces a choice I do not enjoy. If the committee cannot defend a solo IceCube award, a mature topological-insulator prize (B028) is a safer single-achievement outcome and I would not oppose it. The 2D-versus-3D credit split in B028 is the cost of that safety.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first as a genuinely new class of quantum matter, mature, with calculation and measured spectra agreeing, and sees Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as defensible but not unique.
responses.response: I agree that B028 is the most mature candidate on the table and that the science is real, which is why it stays as my first alternative. But your own caveat is the problem: if the trio is 'defensible but not unique', then Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (outside the credited names) and Hasan are all live claims, and the prize is easier to get wrong than the others. I also ask whether a prize two years after the 2016 recognition of topological phases is as new as it feels. I would rather see the committee weigh that than assume it is overdue.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that topological insulators extend the 2016 prize without duplicating it, built on a simple, general Z2 mechanism, and would take the two theorists plus the first decisive experiment.
responses.response: The elegance of the Z2 argument is not in dispute, and I like your sceptical note that Hasan is a defensible alternative for the 3D materials. My disagreement is about novelty. A mechanism that is simple and general is also one that the 2016 citation partly reached, and I would like the committee to say clearly what the prize adds that 2016 did not. I do not think 'rigorously analysable' is itself a Nobel criterion. Nature has to have said something, and in B028 it said it through HgTe and ARPES, which is why I would pair Molenkamp or Hasan with Kane if we go that way.

responses.point: Pearce also ranks IceCube first, valuing a detector-driven discovery with years of calibration, but notes that a one-person configuration may be criticised as incomplete given AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal.
responses.response: We agree on the science, and I appreciate that you state the credit problem plainly rather than leaving it to the rest of us. My answer is that Halzen conceived the cubic-kilometre concept and the science case and led the collaboration through to the 2013 result, so the achievement is traceable to a person, even if the detector was a collective effort. The Nobel statutes allow us to name a discovery and a person, and the citation I propose names the discovery. I accept that the committee should test whether anyone else on the IceCube side has a claim we cannot see in the supplied names. As you note, only Halzen is credited, so the alternative of dropping B005 for B028 remains open.

responses.point: Kroll and Lindroth rank optical lattice clocks first: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's demonstrations took timekeeping to 10^-18, opening tests of redshift and varying constants and a redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I respect the measurement quality, and a clock that sees gravitational redshift across millimetres is a beautiful instrument. But as Secretary I keep asking what the discovery is. So far the new observables you list are prospects, not results, and the 2005 and 2012 prizes already honoured the comb and ion-clock control. I could change my mind if someone shows me a concrete finding from the lattice clocks that nature did not allow us to guess. For now I rank this below the neutrino and moire candidates.

responses.point: Olsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first and proposes Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Andrei, arguing Andrei's STM work showed flat-band signatures earlier and independently, while Bistritzer would be left out.
responses.response: Your point about Andrei's earlier STM evidence is fair and I take it seriously, and I do not think the record should be written as if only the 2018 transport papers existed. I still lean to MacDonald over Bistritzer-or-Andrei only because the prize here is shared with another achievement and the ceiling is three people. That is an artefact of my configuration, not a verdict on Bistritzer's claim, which I regard as strong. If B046 stands alone, I would revert to Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer for the theory-led prediction, and I would want us to examine your Andrei argument properly, because a three-person prize cannot hide a priority dispute.

uncertainties: Whether a solo IceCube award can be defended against the AMANDA, DUMAND, Baikal and wider IceCube collaboration claims; only Halzen is credited in the supplied data.
Whether the committee prefers one achievement with three names (for example B046 alone, which has the broadest support) over my two-part configuration.
Who among MacDonald, Bistritzer and Andrei should hold the second moire seat once a three-person ceiling applies to the whole prize.
Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism makes twisted bilayer graphene premature compared with the mature topological-insulator case.
My recall of IceCube source-association and priority details is from memory and has not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. My ties are to David Gross (my PhD supervisor), Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala string group, and none of them is connected to a shortlisted name. I work on string theory and cosmology, so I am not a specialist in condensed matter or neutrino detectors and defer to colleagues on technical detail.
